HERODIAN · 1.112

Accent examples, with their qualifications

Look up forms actually printed in this passage: -ωος with iota, -υιος, simple -αος forms, and the named exceptions.

Accepts accented or unaccented Greek, including Κωιος for Κῷος. One word at a time. Results reproduce the source’s examples.

Attested accentuation

—

Read the rule with its exceptions

προπερισπᾶται means a circumflex on the penult: the first syllable of a disyllable such as Κῷος. The -ωος exceptions κλῳός, ζῳός and Τρῳός are oxytone.

The passage limits its statement about Attic omission of iota to the -υιος examples. For σῷος, it separately contrasts Didymus’s iota spelling with the traditional spelling without iota.

For simple trisyllables in -αος, the oxytone pattern is qualified by the quantity of the antepenult and by consonant separation. ἵλαος and Πίταος are named exceptions. The source has a gap after these examples; this explorer does not fill it.

Θήβαος, ἄρχαος, Ἄλκαος, πάλαος and Ἄχαος are identified as Aeolic forms lacking iota. Their printed accents are retained.

Source: Περὶ καθολικῆς προσῳδίας 1.112 · attested examples. This lookup does not infer an accent for unlisted words.

original.english_translation: Disyllables in -ωος with iota written in addition are accented with a circumflex on the antepenult: Κῷος, the citizen of Cos; σῷος, which Didymus says is to be written with iota, though the tradition knows it without the iota; Λῷος; Πτῷος, of Acraephiae and Euxippe. But κλῳός, from κλοιός, is accented with an acute, and likewise ζῳός and Τρῳός. Forms in -υιος, being rare, are accented with an acute: υἱός and γυιός; and the Attics write these without the iota. Simple trisyllables in -ος, with only α in the penult, are accented with an acute, unless the third syllable from the end is long by nature or position, or has a consonant by separation: ἀγλαός; ἀλαός from ἀλῶ ‘I wander’: ἀλαός, ‘the one who wanders about’. Seleucus, however, derives it from ἀλάσαι, which means ‘to diminish’, so that it is ‘one whose eyes have been diminished’; others, ‘the blind man’, deprived of λᾶειν, that is, of seeing. Aristarchus interprets the poet’s «ἀσπαίροντα λάων» (Od. τ 229) in this way, in the sense of ‘seeing’. κεραός; ταναός. Δαναός, the citizen, with the same sound as the founder. Κραναός, from whom Attica was called Κραναή. Μαλαός, who founded Temnus, a city of Aeolis. But ἵλαος and Πίταος, a Phrygian, friend of Midas, have the third syllable from the end long. But … has a consonant by separation. And γόαος has come from γόης. But Θήβαος, ἄρχαος, Ἄλκαος, πάλαος, Ἄχαος, formed through lack of iota, are Aeolic.

Based (loosely) on Aelius Herodianus, Περὶ καθολικῆς προσῳδίας 1.112. Type a Greek word and see a playful “rule-based” accent suggestion.

Mini-cheat sheet (from the passage, simplified)
  • Disyllables in -ωος with written ι (e.g. Κῷος) → circumflex (toy places it on the first vowel).
  • But some -ωος are acute: κλῳός, ζῳός, Τρῳός (toy treats these as a small exception list).
  • -υιος (rare) → acute: υἱός, γυιός; Attic often writes without ι.
  • Simple trisyllables in -ος with only α in the penult (…-α-ος) → acute, unless the antepenult is “long” (toy can’t really scan quantity, so it just flags likely long vowels like η/ω/αι/ει/ου).
  • Aeolic “lack of ι”: forms like Θήβαος, ἄρχαος etc. (toy just labels them).

This is a toy: it does not implement full Greek accentuation or syllable quantity. It’s meant to make the patterns in 1.112 feel tangible.
